I've been working this land since I was a young man. My father grew wheat and corn here, and his father before him. That's what the soil here is good for, that's what the grain station buys, and that's what I know how to do well. I'm not going to try something new at 54. The risk isn't worth it — I have no extra money to gamble with if a new crop fails.

I have about 10 mu of flat irrigated land. The rotation is fixed in my head: winter wheat goes in after the autumn harvest, then summer corn goes right in after the wheat comes off in June. Same 10 mu, two crops a year. This is what every family on my street does.

For wheat, I'll use the Jimai variety — the seed station recommends it and my neighbor has gotten good results for three years. I put down phosphate and urea as base fertilizer when I rotary-till before seeding, then I come back with a bag of urea at jointing stage. I pump from the well four times: once at sowing if it's dry, once before winter sets in, once at jointing, once at heading. I spray herbicide in early spring, then watch for aphids and rust in April — if I see them I spray again.

For corn, I buy hybrid seed — always hybrid, you can't save it but the yield is much better. I direct-seed right after wheat harvest, no time to till properly. Base fertilizer goes in with the planter, then I broadcast urea at the big flare stage. Corn here doesn't need as much water — I'll pump once at establishment if it hasn't rained, once more at silking if it's really dry.
